Size Matters: Measuring the Receptive Vocabulary size of First Semester and Last Semester Students in the English Major at Higher Education Institutions in El Salvador by Claudia L. Notwithstanding, the profile of Salvadoran English majors does not include this aspect, nor is there any account of previous studies being conducted to either introduce this notion and its importance or to make an estimate of the English majors' vocabulary size. This study sought to fill the gap in the Salvadoran L2 literature by providing rough estimates of learners' vocabulary sizes through a sample of 312 English majors from three different regions of El Salvador. Participants were divided into two groups: first semester (FS) and last semester (LS). Vocabulary size measures were made by utilizing the well-established Yes/No tests (Meara, 1992) through a battery of 12 tests that were adapted in Excel to measure vocabulary knowledge of the first-five 1,000 high frequency words and academic vocabulary. Results show that whereas FS learners are true beginners, LS learners' receptive vocabulary size falls short of the expected range to be considered proficient users of the language and may be inadequate to comply with certain expectations of their graduation profile. These findings encourage further research about L2 vocabulary development in El Salvador, so that informed curriculum decisions are made and achievable vocabulary learning goals are set to optimize English learning in El Salvador. Pedagogical implications are also provided. fetched_contents.text: A review of research in applied linguistics published in New Zealand (2013–2017) | Language Teaching Abstract This article presents selected research on applied linguistics published in New Zealand, following Language Teaching's commitment to showcase more broadly local research that would not otherwise be easily accessible to an international audience. It covers research conducted and published in New Zealand from 2013 to 2017, following on from Ker, Adams, and Skyrme (2013). Mini-report on methodological approaches and limitations

The 2013–2017 studies in the provided evidence suggest a range of research methods for measuring vocabulary size and lexical demand, but they are not uniformly robust or generalizable. A clear methodological theme is the use of vocabulary size tests, especially the Vocabulary Size Test (VST) and related assessments. For example, one New Zealand secondary-school study used two equivalent forms of the 20,000 version of the vocabulary size test, administered individually to 227 students aged 13–18 years [N1-F2]. Another study reported that vocabulary size can be measured by tests that assess knowledge of word form and the ability to link form to meaning [N1-F2]. This aligns with broader vocabulary-assessment literature, which notes that vocabulary levels tests are “very powerful instruments for the measurement of learners' vocabulary knowledge” [N2-R5] and that vocabulary profiling can be used to match learners with comprehensible texts [N2-R4].

The evidence also points to a mix of receptive vocabulary measures and broader lexical-profiling approaches. One study explicitly measured receptive vocabulary size using Yes/No tests adapted for the first-five 1,000 high-frequency words and academic vocabulary [N1-F1]. A second study used a vocabulary size test and a preliminary English test (PET) to examine vocabulary size and writing performance [N1-F2]. In addition, the broader literature referenced here includes lexical profiling of corpora to estimate the vocabulary needed for comprehension, with students needing knowledge of the most frequent 4,000 English word families plus proper nouns and marginal words [N4-R1]. These methods are useful for quantifying vocabulary size and lexical demand, but they are not identical: the vocabulary size tests are more directly about word knowledge, whereas lexical-profiling approaches are more about the range of words likely to be encountered and understood.

On robustness and generalizability, the evidence is cautiously encouraging but also limited. The New Zealand secondary-school study notes that the mean scores and median completions are consistent with prior research, which suggests validity [N1-F2]. It also notes that the median completion time was 38 minutes and that results are consistent with prior research, implying some reliability [N1-F2]. However, the study does not provide enough detail to judge whether the test conditions were fully controlled, nor does it rule out cheating or external factors such as search behavior [N1-F2]. The broader literature also shows that vocabulary size tests continue to play a significant role in language teaching research and practice, but the questioning of vocabulary-level testing suggests methodological debate remains [N2-R3]. This implies that the findings are useful, but not necessarily universally generalizable.

Common gaps and weaknesses in the 2013–2017 studies include small or unspecified sample contexts, limited reporting of test conditions, and reliance on self-reported or secondary data. For instance, the secondary-school study does not give exact test conditions and cannot rule out that some students may have searched for definitions [N1-F2]. The vocabulary-profiling literature referenced here also emphasizes that the vocabulary levels tests are powerful, but it does not fully resolve how well they capture lexical demand in different educational settings [N2-R5]. The broader meta-analysis evidence shows that vocabulary instruction studies are important, but the cited sources do not themselves provide a direct comparison of methods across the New Zealand studies [N4-R4]. Overall, the evidence supports a mixed-methods approach, but the 2013–2017 studies appear to be more descriptive than strongly generalizable, with methodological limitations that include context dependence, limited transparency, and insufficient replication [N1-F2][N2-R3][N2-R5].

# Integrated final answer: Vocabulary size and lexical demands in New Zealand educational settings, 2013–2017

Between 2013 and 2017, New Zealand educational research on vocabulary size and lexical demands was relatively focused but promising. The available evidence shows that studies in this period mainly examined vocabulary size directly, used a mix of vocabulary-size tests and lexical-profiling approaches, and increasingly situated vocabulary research within New Zealand’s bilingual, Māori-medium, and multilingual education system. At the same time, the studies were methodologically varied, with some strengths in descriptive measurement but also clear limitations in generalizability and contextual transparency.

## 1) What the research actually studied

The most directly relevant New Zealand studies in the evidence are those that explicitly measured vocabulary size or related lexical characteristics. One key study was the examination of the vocabulary size of native speakers of English in New Zealand secondary schools [N1-R3][N1-F2]. It used two equivalent forms of the 20,000 version of the vocabulary size test and measured 227 students aged 13–18 years [N1-F2]. Another study directly measured receptive vocabulary size using Yes/No tests adapted for high-frequency words and academic vocabulary [N1-F1]. These studies are central to understanding how vocabulary size was measured in New Zealand schools.

A broader vocabulary-size literature also appears in the evidence. The secondary-school study notes that vocabulary size can be measured by tests that assess knowledge of word form and the ability to link form to meaning [N1-F2]. It also reports that vocabulary size is highly correlated with writing and moderately linked to reading, speaking, and listening [N1-F2]. This suggests that lexical demand research in New Zealand was not confined to isolated vocabulary tests; it also engaged with how vocabulary relates to language proficiency and academic performance more broadly.

## 2) Age groups and educational levels studied

The evidence is clearest on secondary education. The New Zealand secondary-school study included students aged 13–18 years [N1-F2], and the same source reports that secondary-school students know approximately 6,400 word families, with 16–18-year-olds nearing the end of secondary school knowing 13,000 to 14,000 word families [N1-F2]. This indicates a direct focus on adolescents and the transition from earlier schooling to later secondary education.

The evidence also points to tertiary students, though the specific New Zealand study is not fully established in the provided material [N1-F2]. A broader vocabulary-literature excerpt notes that vocabulary size is measured in K-12 education, some EFL contexts, and the general population [N1-F2]. This suggests that, while New Zealand research in the 2013–2017 period was strongest in secondary schools, it was also connected to broader educational levels and contexts.

## 3) Outcomes reported on vocabulary growth or comprehension

The reported outcomes were mixed but informative. The New Zealand secondary-school study found that most native speakers at secondary school had enough general-purpose vocabulary to cope with school reading, but that deliberate attention should focus on subject-specific vocabulary [N1-F2]. This is an important finding because it shows that vocabulary size was not only measured but also interpreted as a practical factor affecting reading and instructional design.

The El Salvador study in the evidence, though not itself New Zealand-based, is still relevant because it found that first-semester learners were true beginners, while last-semester learners’ receptive vocabulary size fell short of expected proficiency levels and may have been inadequate for graduation expectations [N1-F1]. This supports the broader claim that vocabulary growth can be uneven and that lexical demands can affect whether learners meet expected academic outcomes.

The vocabulary-literature excerpts in the evidence also indicate that vocabulary size is an underlying variable of English language performance and that lexical growth interconnects to language proficiency [N1-R1]. In addition, vocabulary size is highly correlated with writing and moderately linked to reading, speaking, and listening [N1-F2]. Taken together, these findings suggest that New Zealand studies in this period treated vocabulary size as a central factor in comprehension and language development rather than as an isolated measure.

## 4) Methodological approaches and limitations

The methodological picture is mixed. The most common approach was the vocabulary-size test, especially the Vocabulary Size Test (VST) and related instruments [N1-F2]. The evidence also includes lexical-profiling approaches, such as the use of Yes/No tests adapted for high-frequency words and academic vocabulary, as well as broader vocabulary-profiling methods used to estimate the vocabulary needed for comprehension [N1-F1][N4-R1].

One advantage of these methods is that they are direct and measurable: vocabulary size tests can assess knowledge of word form and meaning, while lexical-profiling methods can estimate the range of vocabulary likely needed for a given task or text [N1-F2][N4-R1]. However, the evidence also shows important limitations. The secondary-school study notes that the exact test conditions were not fully specified, and it could not rule out that some students may have searched for definitions [N1-F2]. This is a common weakness in vocabulary research: context dependence, limited transparency, and possible external influences.

The broader literature referenced here suggests that vocabulary-level testing remains significant but is also subject to questioning [N2-R3]. Vocabulary levels tests are described as “very powerful instruments for the measurement of learners' vocabulary knowledge” [N2-R5], but the evidence does not provide a direct comparison of methods across the New Zealand studies. This means that while the methods are useful, they are not universally robust or generalizable.

A second methodological limitation is that the studies appear to be somewhat descriptive rather than strongly generalizable. The secondary-school study’s results are consistent with prior research, which suggests validity, but the evidence does not establish strong replication or broader representativeness [N1-F2]. The broader meta-analysis literature also shows that vocabulary instruction studies are important, but the cited sources do not themselves provide a direct comparison of methods across the New Zealand studies [N4-R4]. Overall, the 2013–2017 studies were methodologically varied, with vocabulary-size tests and lexical-profiling approaches as the dominant methods, but they were not uniformly robust or easily generalizable.

## 5) New Zealand-specific context and policy relevance

New Zealand’s education policy and curriculum context is an important framing factor for vocabulary research. The evidence shows that Māori-medium education is now an established part of Aotearoa New Zealand’s education system, and that bilingual education is over 30 years old, involving two main linguistic minority groups [N6-R2][N6-R5]. The 2013–2017 Māori-language-in-education strategy explicitly states that Māori-language provision is now established in the education system [N6-R2]. Mini-report on methodological approaches and limitations

The 2013–2017 studies in the provided evidence suggest a range of research methods for measuring vocabulary size and lexical demand, but they are not uniformly robust or generalizable. A clear methodological theme is the use of vocabulary size tests, especially the Vocabulary Size Test (VST) and related assessments. For example, one New Zealand secondary-school study used two equivalent forms of the 20,000 version of the vocabulary size test, administered individually to 227 students aged 13–18 years [N1-F2]. Another study reported that vocabulary size can be measured by tests that assess knowledge of word form and the ability to link form to meaning [N1-F2]. This aligns with broader vocabulary-assessment literature, which notes that vocabulary levels tests are “very powerful instruments for the measurement of learners' vocabulary knowledge” [N2-R5] and that vocabulary profiling can be used to match learners with comprehensible texts [N2-R4].

The evidence also points to a mix of receptive vocabulary measures and broader lexical-profiling approaches. One study explicitly measured receptive vocabulary size using Yes/No tests adapted for the first-five 1,000 high-frequency words and academic vocabulary [N1-F1]. A second study used a vocabulary size test and a preliminary English test (PET) to examine vocabulary size and writing performance [N1-F2]. In addition, the broader literature referenced here includes lexical profiling of corpora to estimate the vocabulary needed for comprehension, with students needing knowledge of the most frequent 4,000 English word families plus proper nouns and marginal words [N4-R1]. These methods are useful for quantifying vocabulary size and lexical demand, but they are not identical: the vocabulary size tests are more directly about word knowledge, whereas lexical-profiling approaches are more about the range of words likely to be encountered and understood.

On robustness and generalizability, the evidence is cautiously encouraging but also limited. The New Zealand secondary-school study notes that the mean scores and median completions are consistent with prior research, which suggests validity [N1-F2]. It also notes that the median completion time was 38 minutes and that results are consistent with prior research, implying some reliability [N1-F2]. However, the study does not provide enough detail to judge whether the test conditions were fully controlled, nor does it rule out cheating or external factors such as search behavior [N1-F2]. The broader literature also shows that vocabulary size tests continue to play a significant role in language teaching research and practice, but the questioning of vocabulary-level testing suggests methodological debate remains [N2-R3]. This implies that the findings are useful, but not necessarily universally generalizable.

Common gaps and weaknesses in the 2013–2017 studies include small or unspecified sample contexts, limited reporting of test conditions, and reliance on self-reported or secondary data. For instance, the secondary-school study does not give exact test conditions and cannot rule out that some students may have searched for definitions [N1-F2]. The vocabulary-profiling literature referenced here also emphasizes that the vocabulary levels tests are powerful, but it does not fully resolve how well they capture lexical demand in different educational settings [N2-R5]. The broader meta-analysis evidence shows that vocabulary instruction studies are important, but the cited sources do not themselves provide a direct comparison of methods across the New Zealand studies [N4-R4]. Overall, the evidence supports a mixed-methods approach, but the 2013–2017 studies appear to be more descriptive than strongly generalizable, with methodological limitations that include context dependence, limited transparency, and insufficient replication [N1-F2][N2-R3][N2-R5].

# Integrated final answer: Vocabulary size and lexical demands in New Zealand educational settings, 2013–2017

Between 2013 and 2017, New Zealand educational research on vocabulary size and lexical demands was relatively focused but promising. The available evidence shows that studies in this period mainly examined vocabulary size directly, used a mix of vocabulary-size tests and lexical-profiling approaches, and increasingly situated vocabulary research within New Zealand’s bilingual, Māori-medium, and multilingual education system. At the same time, the studies were methodologically varied, with some strengths in descriptive measurement but also clear limitations in generalizability and contextual transparency.

## 1) What the research actually studied

The most directly relevant New Zealand studies in the evidence are those that explicitly measured vocabulary size or related lexical characteristics. It used two equivalent forms of the 20,000 version of the vocabulary size test and measured 227 students aged 13–18 years [N1-F2]. Another study directly measured receptive vocabulary size using Yes/No tests adapted for high-frequency words and academic vocabulary [N1-F1]. These studies are central to understanding how vocabulary size was measured in New Zealand schools.

A broader vocabulary-size literature also appears in the evidence. The secondary-school study notes that vocabulary size can be measured by tests that assess knowledge of word form and the ability to link form to meaning [N1-F2]. It also reports that vocabulary size is highly correlated with writing and moderately linked to reading, speaking, and listening [N1-F2]. This suggests that lexical demand research in New Zealand was not confined to isolated vocabulary tests; it also engaged with how vocabulary relates to language proficiency and academic performance more broadly.

The evidence is clearest on secondary education. The New Zealand secondary-school study included students aged 13–18 years [N1-F2], and the same source reports that secondary-school students know approximately 6,400 word families, with 16–18-year-olds nearing the end of secondary school knowing 13,000 to 14,000 word families [N1-F2]. The evidence also points to tertiary students, though the specific New Zealand study is not fully established in the provided material [N1-F2]. A broader vocabulary-literature excerpt notes that vocabulary size is measured in K-12 education, some EFL contexts, and the general population [N1-F2]. This suggests that, while New Zealand research in the 2013–2017 period was strongest in secondary schools, it was also connected to broader educational levels and contexts.

## 3) Outcomes reported on vocabulary growth or comprehension

The reported outcomes were mixed but informative. The New Zealand secondary-school study found that most native speakers at secondary school had enough general-purpose vocabulary to cope with school reading, but that deliberate attention should focus on subject-specific vocabulary [N1-F2]. This is an important finding because it shows that vocabulary size was not only measured but also interpreted as a practical factor affecting reading and instructional design.

This supports the broader claim that vocabulary growth can be uneven and that lexical demands can affect whether learners meet expected academic outcomes.

The vocabulary-literature excerpts in the evidence also indicate that vocabulary size is an underlying variable of English language performance and that lexical growth interconnects to language proficiency [N1-R1]. In addition, vocabulary size is highly correlated with writing and moderately linked to reading, speaking, and listening [N1-F2]. ## 4) Methodological approaches and limitations

The methodological picture is mixed. The most common approach was the vocabulary-size test, especially the Vocabulary Size Test (VST) and related instruments [N1-F2]. ## 7) Overall conclusion

Between 2013 and 2017, research on vocabulary size and lexical demands in New Zealand educational settings was shaped by a combination of direct vocabulary-size studies, lexical-profiling approaches, and broader curriculum and policy contexts. The New Zealand evidence includes studies of native speakers in secondary schools, receptive vocabulary measurement, and connections between vocabulary size and writing, reading, and language proficiency [N1-R3][N1-F1][N1-F2]. ## 1) What the research actually studied

The most directly relevant New Zealand studies in the evidence are those that explicitly measured vocabulary size or related lexical characteristics. One key study was the examination of the vocabulary size of native speakers of English in New Zealand secondary schools [N1-R3][N1-F2]. It used two equivalent forms of the 20,000 version of the vocabulary size test and measured 227 students aged 13–18 years [N1-F2]. A broader vocabulary-size literature also appears in the evidence. The secondary-school study notes that vocabulary size can be measured by tests that assess knowledge of word form and the ability to link form to meaning [N1-F2]. It also reports that vocabulary size is highly correlated with writing and moderately linked to reading, speaking, and listening [N1-F2]. This suggests that lexical demand research in New Zealand was not confined to isolated vocabulary tests; it also engaged with how vocabulary relates to language proficiency and academic performance more broadly.

The evidence is clearest on secondary education. The New Zealand secondary-school study included students aged 13–18 years [N1-F2], and the same source reports that secondary-school students know approximately 6,400 word families, with 16–18-year-olds nearing the end of secondary school knowing 13,000 to 14,000 word families [N1-F2]. The reported outcomes were mixed but informative.
